title: p99/p95 tail latency deep dive with Catalyst Systems
summary: Deep dive focused on p95/p99 tail latency for Catalyst Systems' low-latency chat inference workloads. Covered streaming vs non-streaming, KV cache warm/cold behavior, batching tradeoffs, quantization impacts, network hops (cross-AZ), and mitigations including dedicated capacity, local KV cache priming, and async streaming. Agreed next steps: run controlled p99 benchmark using 5K synthetic requests, share benchmark template and security pack, schedule pilot on Redwood Dedicated in their us-west-2 region.

transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-11-18
- Start: 15:00 PST
- Duration: ~62 minutes
- Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Jia Chen (Redwood SE), Alicia Gomez (Redwood SE), Maya Thompson (Catalyst CTO), Leo Alvarez (Catalyst ML), Priya Desai (Catalyst Infra), Ethan Park (Catalyst SRE)

Auto-summary (auto): deep dive on tail latency sources and mitigations; action items to run benchmarks and schedule pilot

[00:00] Samir Patel: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda: we want to walk through p95/p99 numbers you're seeing, root causes, streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs, kv cache behavior, batching, quantization, and network hops. welcome, maya, leo, priya.

[00:27] Maya Thompson: thanks, samir. yeah we've been seeing sporadic p99 spikes up to 1.8s for our 8k-context chat flows and p95 around 420ms; median is fine. main thing is user-facing spikes in the product.

[00:42] Jia Chen: 1.8 seconds on p99 for an 8k flow, got it. are those streaming responses or full response wait?

[00:48] Leo Alvarez: mostly non-streaming in our frontend — we buffer server side then render. we do have a streaming option but it's not enabled for all routes cuz of ordering complexity.

[01:05] Alicia Gomez: quick clarifying q: when you say 8k context, is that token count or char?

[01:09] Leo Alvarez: token count. avg turn length 300 tokens, but system prompt + history pushes seq to ~6k-8k.

[01:22] Samir Patel: ok good. two buckets of tail sources: runtime/compute (kv cache misses, batching delays, quantization slow-paths) and network/orchestration (cross-AZ hops, cold start on model shards, scheduling jitter). we'll step through each.

[01:42] Priya Desai: our infra is multi-AZ in us-west-2. we see spikes correlate with deployments and sometimes when autoscaler kicks in.

[01:51] Jia Chen: that makes sense. autoscaling can cause capacity churn; if requests hit a pod with a cold KV cache (empty KV), the first few tokens incur memory population costs. for decoder-only models, kv warm/cold is big.

[02:10] Ethan Park: small point — our VPC peering adds a hop to the control plane in a different AZ, and sometimes DNS resolution delays add ~40-60ms.

[02:21] Samir Patel: yep, network hops add up. cross-AZ RTTs and NAT/gateway queuing can amplify p99. in our experience, keeping inference and control plane in the same AZ reduces jitter.

[02:36] Maya Thompson: can you explain the streaming vs non-streaming differences re: tail latency? we assumed streaming always reduces tail.

[02:44] Jia Chen: short answer: streaming helps perceived latency for the user because first tokens get back quickly, but it doesn't eliminate p99 for completion latency if the model still needs to compute many tokens. also, streaming opens different failure modes (backpressure on sockets, chunk reassembly). non-streaming can show worse p99 because client waits until the end; but if you chunk early and flush partial outputs you get the best of both.

[03:05] Leo Alvarez: so for us, switching to streaming might reduce the number of user visible timeouts, but our backend logic expects full payloads for ranking; we'd need to adapt.

[03:18] Samir Patel: yep, that's common. other levers: prefix KV caching for common system prompts, shard-local KV priming, and small batching windows to avoid long queue times.

[03:30] Priya Desai: curious about batching — we thought bigger batches always mean better throughput and lower cost, but could worsen tail latency?

[03:37] Jia Chen: exactly. batching increases throughput but also creates queuing delay — if you wait X ms to fill a batch, that adds to per-request latency. dynamic batching that caps wait time (e.g., 5-10ms) often yields good p95 while preserving throughput. but p99 can still spike when batch sizes or seq lengths vary widely.

[04:00] Alicia Gomez: transcription note: "K V cache" sometimes written as KV-cache in the logs — the automated transcription mangles that, sorry.

[04:07] Samir Patel: no problem. quantization also shows up: int8 vs int4 on certain kernels can reduce compute time but some ops fall back to FP16 slower paths on certain kernels/hardware. that fallback causes outlier latency.

[04:24] Leo Alvarez: are there concrete numbers for int8 vs fp16 on p99?

[04:27] Jia Chen: rough numbers from our internal tests: median token latency on int8 ~20% lower, p99 however can be 5-15% worse when fallbacks occur due to mismatched kernels or long sequences. so quantization isn't free — need tuned kernels and profiling.

[04:45] Maya Thompson: we also saw GC pauses in one of our Python request handlers — might be unrelated but suspicious.

[04:52] Ethan Park: yes we patch and saw ~100-200ms spikes occasionally from worker restarts.

[04:57] Samir Patel: lifecycle of a request: client -> LB -> inference node -> control plane (auth/logging) -> model shard. each hop adds variance. suggestion: collocate control plane endpoints or use local caches for auth tokens to avoid sync calls on the hot path.

[05:20] Leo Alvarez: do you support on-prem / private deployments so we can keep everything inside our VPC?

[05:26] Samir Patel: yes, Redwood Private and Dedicated allow VPC and on-prem options. Dedicated is reserved GPU pools we manage in your VPC; Private is customer-controlled. both reduce cross-tenant noise and can improve tail. note that Dedicated still needs network connectivity for control plane unless you run Private fully on-prem.

[05:45] Priya Desai: for compliance we prefer VPC-peered dedicated clusters. what are the latency SLOs you can hit for p99 with Dedicated?

[05:54] Jia Chen: it depends on model size and context length. for a 13B open-model with 8k context, we've seen p95 ~350-500ms and p99 ~800-1000ms on well-tuned Dedicated setups with KV warm caches and local shards. if you stream, user-perceived latency for first tokens can be <200ms.

[06:15] Maya Thompson: that p99 is still high for us in some flows — we target sub-500ms p99 for interactive chat. is that realistic?

[06:23] Samir Patel: sub-500ms p99 for 8k is tough but not impossible: you'd need aggressive quantization working end-to-end with tuned kernels, local primed KV cache for common prompts, tiny batching windows, and very local networking (same AZ, dedicated capacity). also consider model distillation or a lower-ctx model for interactive routes.

[06:44] Leo Alvarez: can we do hybrid route: interactive path uses distilled model with small context and fall back to full model for long-form or archival items?

[06:52] Jia Chen: that's a good pattern — dual-tier models and routing policies. Redwood supports smart routing: route by latency and cost policies, and fallback to the larger model asynchronously.

[07:02] Alicia Gomez: quick aside: there was a note in the logs where "Redwood Dedicate" was spelled weird in the transcript — ignore that.

[07:08] Priya Desai: how do KV cache warmups work on cold restarts? can we pre-warm?

[07:13] Jia Chen: yes, you can prime KV caches with representative prefixes or recent hot requests. we provide priming APIs in our runtime; SEs can share scripts. priming reduces the first-batch token cost dramatically. also keep a small warm pool of model workers to absorb spikes — a reserved hot pool.

[07:35] Ethan Park: any concerns about memory usage with priming? we have limited GPU RAM on some nodes.

[07:40] Jia Chen: priming increases KV memory usage but it's a tradeoff; we can tune retained context length or evict LRU entries. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization and priming size by workload.

[07:52] Samir Patel: let's look at a concrete example — customer reported p95 420ms, p99 1.8s. potential contributors: 1) cross-AZ hops adding ~100-200ms to a subset, 2) cold KV misses on some pods, 3) large batch occasionally triggered by a spike in concurrent requests, 4) kernel fallback from quantization on long seqs, 5) orchestration churn from autoscaling. any logs you can share?

[08:18] Maya Thompson: yes attached a sample trace in the deck — it's named "trace_20261112.zip" we shared earlier.

[08:23] Samir Patel: great — can Jia run that trace through our p99 profiler and correlate with kernel fallbacks?

[08:28] Jia Chen: yeah we'll ingest the trace and look for timing per-hop; I expect to see a subset with cross-AZ RTT and one with shard cold start.

[08:36] Leo Alvarez: about batching windows — what do you recommend for chat workloads?

[08:40] Jia Chen: for chat, very small batching windows (<10ms) and dynamic batching by sequence-length binning works well. you can also separate small interactive requests into a low-latency queue and bulk requests into a high-throughput queue.

[08:55] Maya Thompson: is there a telemetry/observability feature we can use to attribute p99 to specific causes? e.g., kv-miss vs network vs kernel fallback?

[09:03] Samir Patel: yes Redwood Console exposes per-token latency breakdowns: queueing, kernel compute, kv-populate, network/hop. and trace hooks to tag requests so you can see cross-AZ RTTs. we can enable detailed traces for the pilot.

[09:18] Ethan Park: any security implications of priming with real user prompts? must mask PII.

[09:23] Alicia Gomez: good call. we recommend synthetic prime prompts or sanitized recent prompts; also KMS for encryption at rest for priming artifacts.

[09:32] Priya Desai: for Dedicated, how does rollout work? we want canary on a small percentage and immediate fallback if p99 increases.

[09:40] Jia Chen: Redwood supports canary rollouts and automatic fallback policies. you can set p99 thresholds per-route that trigger immediate traffic shift.

[09:48] Samir Patel: quick note on network: NAT gateways and shared egress can introduce jitter. if possible, use ENI or private IP paths for intra-region traffic. also shorten TLS handshake on hot paths with connection reuse.

[10:05] Maya Thompson: any guidance on acceptable batch sizes for 13B vs 70B?

[10:09] Jia Chen: 13B tolerates larger batch sizes; 70B often needs smaller batches due to memory constraints and longer compute per token. the bigger the model, the more careful you need to be with batch-induced queuing.

[10:22] Leo Alvarez: what's a good experiment to isolate network vs runtime?

[10:25] Samir Patel: run a colocated micro-benchmark: generate requests from a client in the same AZ as the inference node and compare to client in other AZs. also run with KV primed vs cold on same node to separate KV cost. we'll provide the harness.

[10:38] Maya Thompson: can you also include a traffic pattern with 95th and 99th percentile concurrency bursts? we have occasional chatroom spikes.

[10:44] Samir Patel: yes the harness supports spike profiles. we'll share config.

[10:50] Priya Desai: on quantization, you mentioned kernel fallbacks — are there hardware combos we should prefer?

[10:56] Jia Chen: NVIDIA H100s with latest cuBLAS/cuDNN + tuned kernels are best for mixed precision. some older A100 drivers have more fallback cases. also some open kernels on other vendors still have edge-case slow paths.

[11:12] Ethan Park: in our logs we saw a lot of small GC pauses — could the language runtime be on the critical path?

[11:17] Samir Patel: yes any non-native layer (Python side) is dangerous on the hot path. best practice: move heavy pre/post processing to async workers or native libraries to keep hot path minimal.

[11:29] Maya Thompson: ok this is super helpful. can you capture recommended runbook steps we can follow to move p99 down?

[11:35] Samir Patel: short runbook: 1) run the p99 benchmark harness across AZs (Samir/Jia) 2) prime KV caches for hot prefixes and maintain small warm pool 3) separate low-latency and bulk queues; small batching windows for low-latency path 4) enable streaming for interactive routes or flush partial tokens 5) use Dedicated in same AZ and prefer H100-like hardware 6) monitor per-token breakdowns in Redwood Console and set p99 alerts 7) consider a distilled model for interactive routes.

[12:00] Leo Alvarez: sounds good. for the pilot, what's the expected timeline?

[12:03] Samir Patel: we can spin up a Dedicated pilot in ~2 weeks pending networking and procurement; first data-driven p99 run within that week.

[12:10] Maya Thompson: procurement note: we'll need SOC2 + encryption docs for Dedicated evaluation.

[12:14] Alicia Gomez: we'll share the security pack and SOC2 report today.

[12:18] Priya Desai: final question: any gotchas for on-prem?

[12:21] Jia Chen: on-prem gives you maximum control over network hops but adds ops overhead. watch out for GPU firmware/network driver mismatches which can cause kernel fallback. we recommend a preflight checklist.

[12:33] Samir Patel: ok let's summarize and close. next steps we listed earlier. thanks everyone.

[12:40] Maya Thompson: thanks all, appreciate the detailed help.

End transcript.
